nameStory: The Blue Orchard Bee gets its name from two key traits: its distinctive metallic blue-black sheen that catches the light beautifully, and its superstar status as an orchard pollinator. Unlike honeybees, these solitary bees are perfectly timed to emerge just as apple, cherry, and other fruit trees burst into bloom, making them incredibly valuable to orchardists.
description: The Blue Orchard Bee is a robust, solitary mason bee with a striking metallic blue-black body that gleams in sunlight. These chunky bees are excellent pollinators, especially for fruit trees, and are much more efficient than honeybees at moving pollen around. Unlike social bees, each female works alone to build her nest in existing holes or hollow stems, creating individual mud-walled chambers for her eggs. They're medium-sized bees, noticeably stockier than honeybees but smaller than carpenter bees.

idTips.label: Metallic blue-black body
idTips.description: The entire body shimmers with a deep metallic blue or blue-black color that's unmistakable in good light - like looking at the wing of a grackle

idTips.label: Chunky, robust build
idTips.description: Much stockier and more barrel-shaped than honeybees, with a thick, powerful-looking body that seems built for hard work

idTips.label: Dark wings
idTips.description: Wings appear dark or smoky rather than clear, creating a nice contrast against the metallic body

idTips.label: Solitary behavior
idTips.description: Always seen working alone, never in groups, often hovering around holes in wood, hollow stems, or bamboo tubes

idTips.label: Mud-gathering behavior
idTips.description: Females can be spotted collecting wet mud or clay in their jaws to build nest partitions - they'll have dirty faces and legs from this work

habitat: Blue Orchard Bees thrive in areas with abundant nesting sites like dead wood, hollow plant stems, or even man-made bee houses near flowering trees and shrubs. They're commonly found in orchards, gardens, forest edges, and suburban areas throughout New England, especially where fruit trees, maples, and willows provide early spring nectar. Look for them around south-facing locations that warm up quickly in spring.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity time! Adults emerge in early spring (March-May) when fruit trees bloom, making this the best time to spot their metallic blue bodies buzzing around blossoms and gathering mud for nests.
seasonality.summer: Activity winds down by early summer as adults complete their nesting duties and die off. You might find evidence of their work in the form of mud-plugged holes in wood or stems.
seasonality.fall: Largely inactive as adults, though larvae are developing inside their mud-walled cells, feeding on pollen provisions left by their mothers.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant, with the next generation overwintering as fully developed adults inside their natal cells, waiting for spring warmth to emerge.

funFact: A single female Blue Orchard Bee can do the pollination work of 100 honeybees when it comes to fruit trees - she's so fuzzy and moves so much pollen on her body that orchardists are increasingly using managed populations of these super-pollinators instead of renting honeybee hives!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark mason bees, but the brilliant metallic blue sheen is distinctive - if it looks like it's wearing metallic blue armor, you've found your Blue Orchard Bee. Carpenter bees are much larger and drill their own holes, while Blue Orchard Bees only use existing cavities.
contextualKnowledge: These bees are increasingly popular with gardeners who buy or build "bee houses" - wooden blocks with drilled holes or bundles of hollow stems that provide nesting sites. Many people are delighted to discover that supporting native bees like this one is often more effective for garden pollination than keeping honeybees.
compareHints: Among New England's mason bees, the Blue Orchard Bee is distinguished by its intense metallic blue coloration - most other Osmia species are darker black, brownish, or have less pronounced metallic sheens. The Horn-faced Mason Bee is similar in behavior but tends to be more black than blue, while the Maine Blueberry Bee is specialized for blueberry flowers rather than tree fruits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's mason bees, the bufflehead stands out primarily due to its enlarged head structure.
Among New England's mason bees, the Horn-faced Mason Bee is the only one with facial horns, making identification straightforward.
Among New England's mason bees, the Taurus Mason Bee can be distinguished from the more common Blue Orchard Bee by its darker coloration and lack of metallic blue-green sheen.
